name: Dichanthium
look_here_first: FIRST FIND A RING OF WHITE HAIRS ON THE VEGETATIVE STEM NODE. Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) frequently has conspicuous node rings and several fingerlike terminal racemes. Silky bluestem (D. sericeum) also has silky hairy spikelet racemes and bearded nodes. Confirm actual sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets with magnification. BOTH installed species are INTRODUCED to Texas, not native restoration grasses.

comparison_lesson.title: Dichanthium two-species field comparison
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: KLEBERG = node white hair ring + multiple fingerlike branches; SERICEUM = silkier compact heads. CONFIRM SPIKELETS, NOT COLOR.
quick_split: Introduced invasive warm-season Kleberg bluestem. Start at the 2–15 thin upright/fingerlike paired-spikelet racemes and examine a RING of conspicuous WHITE HAIRS at stem nodes, which is especially useful in this species. Magnify sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets, the awn and lower glume; a hairy pinkish head alone is not species proof.

Introduced SILKY BLUESTEM (not a native Texas bluestem). Examine the silvery-hairy flowering head and narrow, often paired racemes, and then magnify the companion sterile/pedicelled spikelet against the awned sessile fertile spikelet. Compare the basal clump and hairy stem nodes against invasive Kleberg bluestem. This photo shows only one small silky head held against fingers, not definitive spikelet dissection.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: No county native certification; Kew states D. annulatum and D. sericeum are introduced in Texas.

field_traits: Often sprawling or creeping via stolonlike lower shoots and eventually ascending erect to about 1 m.
A prominent node collar of WHITE HAIRS is a signature feature; must be photographed at node, not assumed from panicle.
Inflorescence of 2–15 fingerlike racemes bearing paired sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets.
Spikelets often silvery or purplish, with hairy axes and awned fertile florets; numbers vary.
Introduced/invasive management grass, NOT native restoration seed.
comparisons.how_to_split: D. sericeum is an introduced silky bluestem also with very hairy silvery flowering branches, but often tufted with shorter rhizomes rather than distinctly stoloniferous. D. annulatum is strongly associated with unmistakable white-ringed stem nodes, and its full flowering head may bear more subdigitate racemes. Distinguish both from Bothriochloa/Schizachyrium with paired-spikelet + glume macro; photo of a red-purple foxtail alone is insufficient.

field_traits: Often tufted perennial to about 1 m, sometimes with short rhizomes; annual/perennial treatments may differ by subspecies.
Culms can have hairy or bearded nodes and narrow linear-lanceolate leaf blades.
Many silky long hairs around spikelet pairs and axes yield pale, sometimes purple, fuzzy appearance.
Sessile fertile spikelet around 4 mm in Flora Zambesiaca treatment; awn twisted, bent, sometimes ~25 mm.
Texas occurrence introduced according to Kew; do not place into local-native dashboard metrics.
comparisons.how_to_split: Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) usually has more clearly 2–15 fingerlike racemes and prominently WHITE-RINGED stem nodes, sometimes a creeping/stoloniferous base. D. sericeum's densely silky hair and narrow racemes are useful orientation cues, NOT decisive alone; mature spikelet, paired sterile companion, node and root base necessary. Both species introduced in Texas.

what_to_teach_crew: First look at actual whole plant habit, not just a detached seedhead.
Photograph collar at blade-sheath junction, intact inflorescence with scale and individual mature spikelets.
Use photo arrows only to direct attention to visible structures; don't manufacture microscopic identifications.
No county native certification; Kew states D. annulatum and D. sericeum are introduced in Texas.
